lessons.theory:
## Introduction

A data structure is a systematic way of organizing and storing data in a computer so that it can be used efficiently. Different types of data structures are suited for different applications. Understanding data structures is fundamental to writing efficient programs.
## Key Concepts

- Data Structure: A way to organize data for efficient access and modification
- Primitive types: int, float, char, pointer — built into the language
- Non-primitive types: arrays, lists, trees, graphs — derived from primitives
- Linear vs Non-linear: Linear structures arrange data sequentially (arrays, linked lists). Non-linear structures arrange data hierarchically (trees, graphs).
- Static vs Dynamic: Static structures have fixed size (arrays). Dynamic structures grow/shrink (linked lists).
- Time Complexity: How runtime grows with input size, measured using Big-O notation
- Space Complexity: How memory usage grows with input size

## Important Formulas

- `Big-O hierarchy: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!)`
- `Array element address: A[i] = Base_Address + (i × size_of_element)`
- `Memory for array: n × sizeof(element)`

## Comparison Tables

### Common Data Structures and Their Operations

| Structure | Access | Search | Insertion | Deletion |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Array | O(1) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Linked List | O(n) | O(n) | O(1)* | O(1)* |
| Stack | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) |
| Queue | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) |
| Hash Table | — | O(1)* | O(1)* | O(1)* |
| BST (balanced) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) |

> * Average case. Worst case may differ.

## Summary

A data structure is a systematic way of organizing and storing data in a computer so that it can be used efficiently. Different types of data structures are suited for different applications. Understanding data structures is fundamental to writing efficient programs.

lessons.title: Asymptotic Notation (Big-O, Omega, Theta)
lessons.overview: Asymptotic notation describes the running time of an algorithm as the input size grows toward infinity. It abstracts away machine-specific constants and focuses on the growth rate. Big-O is the most commonly used notation in practice.
keyConcepts: Big-O (O): Upper bound — the algorithm runs in AT MOST this time. f(n) = O(g(n)) means f grows no faster than g.
Big-Omega (Ω): Lower bound — the algorithm runs in AT LEAST this time. f(n) = Ω(g(n)) means f grows at least as fast as g.
Big-Theta (Θ): Tight bound — the algorithm runs in EXACTLY this time. f(n) = Θ(g(n)) means f grows at the same rate as g.
Best case: The minimum time for any input of size n
Worst case: The maximum time for any input of size n
Average case: The expected time averaged over all possible inputs
formulas: If f(n) = aₙnᵏ + aₙ₋₁nᵏ⁻¹ + ... + a₀, then f(n) = O(nᵏ)
Drop constants: O(3n) = O(n)
Drop lower-order terms: O(n² + n) = O(n²)
Logarithm base change: log₂(n) = log(n) / log(2), so O(log₂n) = O(log n)

commonMistakes: Saying O(2n) instead of O(n) — constants are dropped
Saying O(n² + n) instead of O(n²) — lower-order terms are dropped
Confusing best case with Big-O (Big-O is typically worst case)
Forgetting that nested loops multiply, not add: O(n × n) = O(n²), not O(2n)
examTips: When analyzing loops: single loop = O(n), nested loops = O(n²), halving loop = O(log n)
For recursive functions, use the Master Theorem or draw a recursion tree
Always simplify: O(3n² + 5n + 100) = O(n²)

practiceQuestions.explanation: The loop variable i doubles each iteration (i *= 2), so it takes log₂(n) iterations to reach n. This is O(log n).

practiceQuestions.question: If f(n) = 5n³ + 2n² + 100, what is O(f(n))?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Drop the constant 5 and lower-order terms 2n² + 100. The dominant term is n³, so O(n³).

practiceQuestions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Binary search halves the search space each iteration. After k iterations, the remaining size is n/2^k. Setting n/2^k = 1 gives k = log₂(n), so O(log n).

lessons.title: Arrays — Operations and Applications
lessons.overview: An array is a collection of elements of the same type stored in contiguous memory locations. Elements are accessed by index (position). Arrays are the simplest and most widely used data structure.
keyConcepts: Declaration: int arr[10] allocates 10 contiguous integers
Indexing: arr[0] is the first element, arr[n-1] is the last
Random access: any element can be accessed in O(1) time using its index
Memory layout: elements are stored at consecutive addresses
Insertion/Deletion at end: O(1). At beginning/middle: O(n) due to shifting
Limitation: fixed size (cannot grow/shrink at runtime)
2D arrays: stored in row-major order in C — arr[i][j] is at address base + (i × columns + j) × size

## Introduction

An array is a collection of elements of the same type stored in contiguous memory locations. Elements are accessed by index (position). Arrays are the simplest and most widely used data structure.
## Key Concepts

- Declaration: int arr[10] allocates 10 contiguous integers
- Indexing: arr[0] is the first element, arr[n-1] is the last
- Random access: any element can be accessed in O(1) time using its index
- Memory layout: elements are stored at consecutive addresses
- Insertion/Deletion at end: O(1). At beginning/middle: O(n) due to shifting
- Limitation: fixed size (cannot grow/shrink at runtime)
- 2D arrays: stored in row-major order in C — arr[i][j] is at address base + (i × columns + j) × size

## Important Formulas

- `Address of arr[i] = base + i × sizeof(type)`
- `Address of arr[i][j] (row-major) = base + (i × columns + j) × sizeof(type)`
- `Total memory = n × sizeof(type)`

## Comparison Tables

### Array Operations and Complexity

| Operation | Time Complexity | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access arr[i] | O(1) | Direct address calculation |
| Search (unsorted) | O(n) | Linear scan |
| Search (sorted) | O(log n) | Binary search |
| Insert at end | O(1) | Just assign arr[n] = value |
| Insert at beginning | O(n) | Shift all elements right |
| Delete from end | O(1) | Just decrement size |
| Delete from beginning | O(n) | Shift all elements left |
| Traverse | O(n) | Visit each element once |

> Insertion/deletion in the middle requires shifting elements.

## Code Examples

### Array Insertion at a Given Position

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int arr[100] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
    int n = 5;          // current size
    int pos = 2;        // insert at index 2
    int value = 25;     // value to insert

    // Step 1: Shift elements right from pos to n-1
    for (int i = n; i > pos; i--) {
        arr[i] = arr[i - 1];
    }

    // Step 2: Insert the new element
    arr[pos] = value;
    n++;  // increment size

    // Output: 10 20 25 30 40 50
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
    return 0;
}
```

Shifting elements from the insertion point to the end takes O(n) time in the worst case (inserting at the beginning).


## Summary

An array is a collection of elements of the same type stored in contiguous memory locations. Elements are accessed by index (position). Arrays are the simplest and most widely used data structure.

lessons.title: Stacks — LIFO Principle and Applications
lessons.overview: A stack is a linear data structure that follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle — the last element added is the first one removed. Think of a stack of plates: you add (push) and remove (pop) from the top only. Stacks are used in function calls, expression evaluation, undo mechanisms, and backtracking algorithms.
keyConcepts: LIFO: Last-In-First-Out — the last element pushed is the first popped
push(x): add element x to the top of the stack
pop(): remove and return the top element
peek()/top(): view the top element without removing it
isEmpty(): check if the stack is empty
Overflow: pushing when the stack is full (array implementation)
Underflow: popping when the stack is empty
Applications: function call stack, expression evaluation, balanced parentheses, undo/redo, DFS
formulas: Array stack: top = -1 means empty. push: arr[++top] = x. pop: return arr[top--]
Maximum size: if top == MAX-1, stack is full (overflow)
Linked list stack: push creates a new head node, pop removes the head node

lessons.overview: A tree is a hierarchical data structure with nodes connected by edges. A binary tree has at most 2 children per node. A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree where left child < parent < right child. BSTs enable O(log n) search, insertion, and deletion when balanced.

Depth of a node: number of edges from root to the node. Height of a tree: max depth.
Binary Tree: each node has 0, 1, or 2 children.
BST Property: left subtree values < node value < right subtree values
Traversals: Inorder (Left-Root-Right), Preorder (Root-Left-Right), Postorder (Left-Right-Root)
Inorder traversal of a BST gives elements in sorted order
Balanced BST: height ≈ log n → O(log n) operations
Unbalanced BST (worst case): height = n → O(n) operations (degrades to linked list)

# Revision Summary — Binary Trees and BST

**One-line definition:** A tree is a hierarchical data structure with nodes connected by edges. A binary tree has at most 2 children per node. A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree where left child < parent < right chil

**Key points:**

- Root: the top node. Parent: a node with children. Child: a node below a parent. Leaf: a node with no children.
- Depth of a node: number of edges from root to the node. Height of a tree: max depth.
- Binary Tree: each node has 0, 1, or 2 children.
- BST Property: left subtree values < node value < right subtree values
- Traversals: Inorder (Left-Root-Right), Preorder (Root-Left-Right), Postorder (Left-Right-Root)

**Important formulas:**

- `Max nodes at level i: 2ⁱ`
- `Max nodes in tree of height h: 2^(h+1) - 1`
- `Min height of n nodes: ⌊log₂(n)⌋`
- `BST search: compare key with node, go left if smaller, right if larger`

**Common mistake to avoid:** Inserting duplicates — decide on a policy (ignore, or count them)

**Memory hook:** Recall the three pillars — definition, working, example.

# Data Structures — Quick Revision

**Subject code:** R23CP2402  
**Semester:** 3  
**Credits:** 5  

## Unit 1: Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms (10%)
### Introduction to Data Structures
A data structure is a systematic way of organizing and storing data in a computer so that it can be used efficiently. Different types of data structures are suited for different applications. Understanding data structures is fundamental to writing efficient programs.

**Formulas:**
- `Big-O hierarchy: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!)`
- `Array element address: A[i] = Base_Address + (i × size_of_element)`
- `Memory for array: n × sizeof(element)`

### Asymptotic Notation (Big-O, Omega, Theta)
Asymptotic notation describes the running time of an algorithm as the input size grows toward infinity. It abstracts away machine-specific constants and focuses on the growth rate. Big-O is the most commonly used notation in practice.

**Formulas:**
- `If f(n) = aₙnᵏ + aₙ₋₁nᵏ⁻¹ + ... + a₀, then f(n) = O(nᵏ)`
- `Drop constants: O(3n) = O(n)`
- `Drop lower-order terms: O(n² + n) = O(n²)`

## Unit 2: Arrays and Linked Lists (20%)
### Arrays — Operations and Applications
An array is a collection of elements of the same type stored in contiguous memory locations. Elements are accessed by index (position). Arrays are the simplest and most widely used data structure.

**Formulas:**
- `Address of arr[i] = base + i × sizeof(type)`
- `Address of arr[i][j] (row-major) = base + (i × columns + j) × sizeof(type)`
- `Total memory = n × sizeof(type)`

### Singly Linked Lists — Dynamic Memory Management
A linked list is a linear data structure where elements (nodes) are connected via pointers. Unlike arrays, linked lists do not require contiguous memory — each node contains data and a pointer to the next node. Linked lists can grow and shrink dynamically at runtime.

**Formulas:**
- `Node: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; }`
- `Memory per node: sizeof(data) + sizeof(pointer) = 4 + 4 = 8 bytes (on 32-bit)`
- `Traversal: start at head, follow next until NULL`

## Unit 3: Stacks and Queues (20%)
### Stacks — LIFO Principle and Applications
A stack is a linear data structure that follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle — the last element added is the first one removed. Think of a stack of plates: you add (push) and remove (pop) from the top only. Stacks are used in function calls, expression evaluation, undo ...

**Formulas:**
- `Array stack: top = -1 means empty. push: arr[++top] = x. pop: return arr[top--]`
- `Maximum size: if top == MAX-1, stack is full (overflow)`
- `Linked list stack: push creates a new head node, pop removes the head node`

### Queues — FIFO Principle and Applications
A queue is a linear data structure that follows the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principle — the first element added is the first one removed. Think of a line at a ticket counter: the person who joins first is served first. Queues are used in scheduling, buffering, BFS, and printer ...

**Formulas:**
- `Array queue: front = -1, rear = -1 (empty). enqueue: arr[++rear] = x. dequeue: return arr[front++]`
- `Circular queue: rear = (rear + 1) % MAX`
- `Queue full (circular): (rear + 1) % MAX == front`

## Unit 4: Searching and Sorting Algorithms (20%)
### Linear Search and Binary Search
Searching is the process of finding a specific element in a data structure. Linear search checks each element sequentially. Binary search repeatedly halves the search space — but requires the data to be sorted. Choosing the right search algorithm dramatically affects performance.

**Formulas:**
- `Binary search iterations: log₂(n) — halving until 1 element remains`
- `Linear search comparisons (average): n/2`
- `Binary search: mid = (low + high) / 2`

### Bubble, Selection, and Insertion Sort
Sorting arranges elements in ascending or descending order. Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent elements. Selection sort finds the minimum and places it first. Insertion sort builds the sorted array one element at a time. All three are O(n²) in the worst case but differ in thei...

**Formulas:**
- `Bubble sort passes: n-1. Comparisons in pass i: n-i-1. Total: n(n-1)/2`
- `Selection sort comparisons: n(n-1)/2. Swaps: n-1 (one per pass).`
- `Insertion sort comparisons: 1 (best) to i (worst) in pass i. Total worst: n(n-1)/2.`

## Unit 5: Trees and Graphs (20%)
### Binary Trees and BST
A tree is a hierarchical data structure with nodes connected by edges. A binary tree has at most 2 children per node. A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree where left child < parent < right child. BSTs enable O(log n) search, insertion, and deletion when balanced.

**Formulas:**
- `Max nodes at level i: 2ⁱ`
- `Max nodes in tree of height h: 2^(h+1) - 1`
- `Min height of n nodes: ⌊log₂(n)⌋`

vivaBank.question: Define Primitive types.
vivaBank.modelAnswer: int, float, char, pointer — built into the language

vivaBank.question: Define Non-primitive types.
vivaBank.modelAnswer: arrays, lists, trees, graphs — derived from primitives

vivaBank.question: What is Big-O notation?
vivaBank.modelAnswer: Big-O describes the upper bound on an algorithm's runtime as input size grows, ignoring constants and lower-order terms.

vivaBank.question: Define a stack.
vivaBank.modelAnswer: A stack is a linear data structure that follows LIFO order — insertion and deletion happen at one end called the top.

vivaBank.question: Define Big-O (O).
vivaBank.modelAnswer: Upper bound — the algorithm runs in AT MOST this time. f(n) = O(g(n)) means f grows no faster than g.

vivaBank.question: Define Big-Omega (Ω).
vivaBank.modelAnswer: Lower bound — the algorithm runs in AT LEAST this time. f(n) = Ω(g(n)) means f grows at least as fast as g.

vivaBank.question: Define Big-Theta (Θ).
vivaBank.modelAnswer: Tight bound — the algorithm runs in EXACTLY this time. f(n) = Θ(g(n)) means f grows at the same rate as g.

vivaBank.question: Define Indexing.
vivaBank.modelAnswer: arr[0] is the first element, arr[n-1] is the last

vivaBank.question: Define Random access.
vivaBank.modelAnswer: any element can be accessed in O(1) time using its index

vivaBank.question: Define Node.
vivaBank.modelAnswer: a struct containing data + a pointer to the next node
